Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tailor
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma, Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
Isaiah was a 33-year-old tailor living in a modest apartment in a bustling urban neighborhood. He had carved a niche for himself, creating beautiful garments that showcased his skill and creativity. Yet, beneath the surface of his vibrant work, he was wrestling with shadows that had emerged following a harrowing event he could never quite shake off. It was a chilly evening when he found himself caught in the chaos of a terrorist attack at a local market, a place where he often sought inspiration for his designs. The memories were both vivid and elusive—while he could picture the vibrant stalls and the laughter of families, the moment the chaos erupted felt like a film playing on an endless loop in his mind. The sound of screams, the rush of bodies, and the acrid smell of smoke all blended into a terrifying cacophony that haunted him.

In the months that followed, the weight of his experience began to shape his life in ways he could never have anticipated. Isaiah felt an overwhelming sense of vulnerability, and as he moved through his daily routines, he found himself constantly scanning for exits, his mind alert to potential threats that others seemed blissfully unaware of. Whenever he entered a new room, his gaze instinctively darted toward the exits, a habit he had developed to shield himself from a danger he could hardly articulate. He was certain that being vigilant was the only way to maintain some semblance of control in a world that felt increasingly unsafe.

At work, his tailoring studio became a paradoxical sanctuary and a prison. While he loved the craft itself, the anxiety it triggered often left him feeling hollow. He would position himself against the wall, stitching together the fabric of others’ lives while feeling completely detached from his own. There were moments when he could recall the event clearly, yet an unsettling numbness enveloped him, as if he were merely an observer of a stranger’s tragedy. Isaiah couldn’t fully grasp the chaos of that day, as parts of the event remained shrouded in a thick fog of memory gaps. It was as if his mind had decided to protect him from the full impact of his trauma, yet this only fueled his frustration.

In an attempt to escape the gnawing discomfort of his thoughts, Isaiah resorted to long hours spent on his phone, diving into games and scrolling through social media. It felt easier to immerse himself in digital worlds where he could forget about the unpredictability of real life. He had come to believe that this distraction was a necessary crutch, a way to evade the anxiety that lurked just beneath the surface. Yet, this strategy came at a cost. As weeks turned into months, his relationships with friends and family began to fray. He found himself picking arguments over trivial matters, seeking conflict as a means to divert his mind from the trauma that loomed like a dark cloud over him. 

Isaiah’s sense of belonging dwindled, and he felt isolated in a crowd. He no longer felt like a part of his community, a sentiment that deepened his feelings of inadequacy. The belief that he was weak permeated his psyche, and he often questioned whether he would ever be able to reclaim the bold spirit he once had. Each day was a battle between the desire to plan for the future and the paralyzing fear of what that future might hold. Making any plans felt futile, as if he were tempting fate itself.

The breaking point came unexpectedly when he found himself overwhelmed during a gathering at a friend’s house. The laughter and chatter felt like a cacophony of reminders of what he had lost, and as he began to feel the familiar panic rise within him, he excused himself and left abruptly. It was in that moment of solitude, staring blankly at the wall of his apartment, that he realized he could no longer navigate this alone. The thought of seeking help both frightened and relieved him. What terrified Isaiah the most was the fear of being perceived as weak or broken, yet a flicker of hope began to emerge. He wanted to reclaim his life, to learn how to exist in the world without the suffocating grip of his trauma. It was this hope that finally pushed him to reach out for support, ready to confront the memories and fears that had ensnared him for far too long.
